extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and professional stand-up comedians and comedy writers
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques and evaluative criteria for generating, selecting, and polishing short stand-up jokes—focused on producing surprising punchlines from personal, specific material and using volume + selection. Suited for writers crafting jokes for stand-up performance or late-night writing rooms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core principle: surprise (set up implied expectation then shatter it)
rubrics_metrics.description: "One of the key foundations of comedy is to set up an implied expectation for the audience, then shatter that expectation." Surprise is the #1 element necessary to trigger human laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every joke should create an implied expectation in the setup and then break it with the punch. Evaluate whether the setup leads the audience to a clear expectation and whether the punch provides an unexpected resolution. Anti-pattern: punchlines that merely restate expectation or follow a predictable path.

rubrics_metrics.name: 1-2-3 Jokes Method — start with stuff close to you
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with stuff close to you. Ask: 1) What is new? 2) What has changed? 3) What have I acquired? These prompts surface fresh, specific material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these three prompts to mine personal life for specifics that feel authentic and are less likely to be generic. When evaluating material, prefer items that answer one of the three prompts. Guidance: prioritize specificity and immediacy (new/changed/acquired) over abstract or second-hand topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the 5 W's for joke building
rubrics_metrics.description: Most jokes are a convergence of two or more clearly defined ideas. Use the journalistic 5 W's: Who? What? Why? Where? When? For each W, generate associations and then look for unexpected matches across categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concretely answer each W for a potential premise; then cross-pair answers from different Ws to surface collisions that can become setups and punches. Scoring guidance: stronger jokes have at least two distinct W elements combined in an unexpected way. Anti-pattern: vague or generic answers to the W's that yield weak, unfocused premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke writing volume: produce many candidates
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional comedy writers crank out 60–150 jokes per day using these techniques. Volume → quality through ruthless selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat joke generation as a numbers game: produce many short candidates, then ruthlessly select and refine the best. Evaluate whether the joke was chosen from a larger pool rather than being the first idea. Anti-pattern: keeping first drafts without testing many alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke anatomy — Premise
rubrics_metrics.description: Premise: the situation/topic you're commenting on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the premise is clear, specific, and relatable enough to justify the setup and punch. The premise should be narrow enough to support a single surprising twist. If the premise is vague, the joke will lack direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke anatomy — Setup
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The setup should lead the audience to a precise implied expectation without giving away the punch. Avoid over-explaining the setup or including details that telegraph the joke's direction. Scoring note: strong setups create a clear expectation in minimal words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke anatomy — Punch
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The punch must deliver an element of surprise that contrasts with the setup's expectation. It should be concise and serve as a payoff. Anti-patterns: punches that are too predictable, too long, or that merely reiterate the setup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke anatomy — Tag
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tags to extend the laugh after the initial punch, building on the joke's logic. Evaluate tags for whether they add additional surprise or merely repeat the punch; good tags escalate or tighten the joke’s premise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common mistake: punchline too predictable
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If listeners can foresee the punch before it lands, the joke will not elicit strong laughter. When evaluating, check predictability by testing with naive readers/performers; revise to increase misdirection or specificity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common mistake: setup gives away too much
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid including details in the setup that steer the audience directly to the punch. Keep the setup lean so the punch can shift perspective. Editing guidance: remove or obscure clues that make the punch obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common mistake: no clear point of view
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedian's POV should be evident—who is speaking and what perspective anchors the joke. Jokes without a clear voice feel generic. When scoring, prefer jokes with a consistent and distinct viewpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common mistake: generic topics (no 'you' in it)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor material tied to the comedian's life or specifics rather than abstract/general topics. Specificity increases uniqueness and punch potential. Anti-pattern: jokes that could be said by anyone and lack personal markers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corley Rubric item 1: setup establishes a clear implied expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the setup establish a clear implied expectation?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Binary/graded check used to evaluate setups: the setup should create an expectation the audience can hold until the punch. If the expectation is fuzzy, the punch will underperform. Use this as the first gate in selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corley Rubric item 2: punch shatters that expectation surprisingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the punch shatter that expectation surprisingly?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for surprise and clarity of the reversal. The punch should not just be different, but should invert or violate the established expectation in a way that is intelligible and funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corley Rubric item 3: topic specific to the comedian's life (new/changed/acquired)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the topic specific to the comedian's life (new/changed/acquired)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the joke draws from personally specific material (answers one of: What is new? What has changed? What have I acquired?). Personal specifics increase authenticity and distinctiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corley Rubric item 4: 5 W's can be answered concretely
rubrics_metrics.description: Could the 5 W's be answered concretely?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure who/what/why/where/when for the joke are concrete details that can be used to sharpen both setup and punch. Vague or evasive answers indicate a weak premise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corley Rubric item 5: joke selected from many candidates (not the first try)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the joke selected from many candidates (not the first try)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preference for jokes that survived a selection process: generated among many and chosen for strength. This criterion favors revision and iteration; penalizes reliance on initial ideas without exploration.
